land.text: the Visconti lordship of Milan and Pavia, raised to a duchy in 1395: Lombardy, the Ossola, the Valtellina and the Ticino valley in Cliopatria's 1402 outline

predecessors.note: Cliopatria has no row for the Visconti lordship before the duchy; the duchy of 1395 is the same Visconti state, so the lordship needs a dossier from the additions batch (see notes).

land.text: Francesco II Sforza died without heirs in 1535; Charles V, claiming the duchy as an imperial fief, took control and invested his son Philip with it by a diploma signed in Brussels on 11 October 1540

successors.note: Cliopatria keeps the Duchy of Milan shape to 1539 and shows the Spanish crown as its neighbour from 1529; the Habsburg duchy of 1535/1540-1796 is the same land under foreign dukes and needs its own dossier or an extension of this one (see notes).

capitals.name: Milan
capitals.note: Infobox capital: Milan; the Ambrosian Republic (1447-1450) also sat at Milan.

correction.text: the Lombard-Piedmontese core of Cliopatria's 1402 shape plus Verona, Vicenza, Bassano and Feltre (Veneto), years 1395-1401; Pisa is not inside the duchy

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1395-1401: Cliopatria starts the duchy only in 1402, after the breakup of Gian Galeazzo's state. At his death he held 'almost the entire Po Valley'; the footnotes of his testament name Verona, Vicenza, Bassano and Feltre beside the Lombard and Piedmontese cities that Cliopatria's 1402 outline already contains. Padua, lost in 1390, and Bologna, only assaulted in 1402, are left out. No area on the page. Pisa, where Gian Galeazzo was 'Lord of Pisa' from 13 February 1399 to 3 September 1402 (infobox), is not drawn inside the duchy: the title is separate from that of Duke of Milan, the testament left Pisa to Gabriele Maria, and republic-of-pisa keeps Pisa a state to 1406; it is recorded as a vassal_start/vassal_end pair (1399-02 to 1402-09). Repair 2026-10-25: the keyframe 1399-1401 'as 1395 plus Pisa' is merged into this one.

37,443 km2 (Lombardy with Brescia, Bergamo, Cremona, Pavia, Parma and Piacenza, the Valtellina, the Ossola, Ticino, western Piedmont). After 'his empire fragmented' the testament gave Giovanni Maria the duchy (Como, Lodi, Cremona, Bergamo, Brescia), Filippo Maria Pavia, Vercelli, Novara, Alessandria, Tortona and the Veneto cities, Gabriele Maria Pisa and Crema; Cliopatria draws the Lombard-Piedmontese lands of all three as one duchy and drops Verona, Vicenza and Pisa. The pages date none of the individual losses. No infobox area (page: only 'largest at the start of the 15th century').

37,466 km2, 22 km2 more than 1402: a boundary refinement, not a conquest. Filippo Maria 'retook the city' of Milan on 16 June 1412 and 'established his rule over Pavia'; the page gives no other territorial change for 1407-1421.

correction.text: the 1422 shape unchanged; years 1421-1426 (Genoa since 1421, Brescia lost at the end of 1426)

keyframe_review.note: 42,919 km2: the 1407 outline plus the Ligurian coast (Genova, Savona, Imperia, part of La Spezia, 5,453 km2). The page's footnote 'Milan controlled Genoa since 1421' starts the shape a year early, and Brescia is lost on 30 December 1426 (Peace of Venice), so the shape holds 1421-1426 and the next keyframe (1427-1428) subtracts Brescia.
New keyframe 1427-1428: the 1422 shape without Brescia, which the Peace of Venice (30 December 1426) gave to Venice; Bergamo and Crema still Milan's until the Venetian governor appears in 1429.

correction.text: the 1429 shape unchanged; years 1429-1439 (the Leventina is lost in 1440, next keyframe)

keyframe_review.note: 35,384 km2: the 1422 outline without Brescia and Bergamo (7,534 km2, the area of those two provinces) and Crema; 'a Venetian governor was established at Bergamo and Crema' in 1429. Genoa stays until the Peace of Cremona (20 November 1441), so the shape holds 1429-1441 although Cliopatria drops Genoa in 1440. From 1440 the Leventina is Uri's, see the next keyframe.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1429 shape less the Leventina; years 1440-1441 (Genoa still held until the Peace of Cremona, 20 November 1441)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1440-1441: the 1429 outline (Genoa included until the Peace of Cremona, 20 November 1441) without the Leventina valley, which 'Uri conquered ... in 1440' (Ticino page). Cliopatria's 1440 shape drops Genoa a year early and keeps the Leventina; the 1440 keyframe below starts in 1442.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1440 shape less the Leventina; years 1442-1447 (to 13 August 1447)

keyframe_review.note: 29,911 km2: the 1429 outline without the Ligurian coast. The Peace of Cremona (20 November 1441) is the page's date for Genoa's independence, so the shape starts in 1442; it ends with Filippo Maria's death on 13 August 1447 (the Ambrosian Republic follows to March 1450), not in 1449. Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1453 shape less the Leventina; years 1450-1462 (Sforza's duchy from March 1450)

keyframe_review.note: The same 29,911 km2 outline as 1440. Cliopatria's Ambrosian row (1450-1452) is wrong in its years: the republic lasted August 1447 to March 1450 ('On 22 March 1450, he had himself declared capitano del popolo'), so Sforza's duchy owns this shape from 1450. Lodi and Piacenza, occupied by Venice during the republic, are drawn inside it although the pages do not say when they came back (by late 1453 at the latest). Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1463 shape less the Leventina; years 1464-1477 (Genoa held 1463-1478 per the page, conquest dated 1464)

keyframe_review.note: 35,364 km2: the 1453 outline plus the Ligurian coast. The Genoa page says the republic was 'held by the Milanese House of Sforza' in 1463-1478 and also that 'in 1464 Milan changed sides, conquered Genoa'; the shape holds 1464-1477. Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1482 shape less the Leventina; years 1478-1487

keyframe_review.note: 29,911 km2: no Genoa. The Genoa page ends the first Sforza lordship in 1478, so the shape starts in 1478 and runs to 1487. Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1492 shape less the Leventina; years 1488-1496

keyframe_review.note: 35,364 km2: Genoa again. The page dates the second Sforza lordship 1488-1499, four years before Cliopatria's 1492 start, so the shape starts in 1488; it ends with the French conquest of 1499. Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

correction.text: the 1497 shape less the Leventina; years 1497-1498 only

keyframe_review.note: 33,694 km2: the 1492 outline less part of the Savona riviera and a few cells of the Grisons and Ticino; none of these is dated or explained on the pages opened. The page says Louis XII 'invaded the Milanese state in 1499, driving out Ludovico il Moro' and was Duke until 1512, so the shape holds 1497-1498 (Ludovico was 'defeated and taken prisoner in Novara in 1500'); Cliopatria's end in 1501 is too late and its gap from 1502 to 1525 is French rule. Repair 2026-10-25: Cliopatria still draws the Leventina inside this shape; Uri conquered it in 1440 (see the 1440 loss), so it is subtracted.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1526 outline used for 1512-1515: the pages do not itemise the duchy of Maximilian Sforza

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 1512-1515: Cliopatria has no Milan shape for the years of Maximilian Sforza ('29 December 1512: Swiss mercenaries installed Maximilian Sforza as Duke of Milan'; 'de facto controlled' by the Swiss cantons until Marignano). The pages give no territorial list, so Cliopatria's 1526 outline (Milan, Pavia, Lodi, Como, Cremona, the Ossola, western Piedmont, without Parma, Piacenza, the Valtellina and most of Ticino) stands in. Parma was taken for the Pope in 1512; both Parma and Piacenza were surrendered by the Pope to Francis in December 1515. Ticino, the Valtellina, Parma and Piacenza had already left the Milanese state in 1500-1512 under French rule (see the December 1512 gain); the duchy is a Swiss protectorate from 1513 to September 1515 (vassal_start/vassal_end).

New keyframe 1521-1525: after Lautrec was 'forced out of Milan' in late November 1521 Francesco II Sforza was 'restored to power' under Imperial and papal protection; the French held Milan again from 26 October 1524 to the Battle of Pavia (23-24 February 1525). The 1526 outline stands in because the page gives no territory list.

correction.text: the 1526 shape unchanged; year 1526 until 24 July (1527-1528 the land is Imperial-held)

keyframe_review.note: 17,570 km2, 59 percent of the 1497 outline: Parma, Piacenza, Brescia, the Valtellina, Massa-Carrara and nearly all of Ticino are gone and Pavia, Cremona, Lodi and Como are trimmed. 'The citadel of Milan fell to Imperial forces on 24 July 1526', so the shape holds January-July 1526 only; Imperial troops held Milan until Sforza 'was permitted to return' (Cambrai, 1529). (Ticino, the Valtellina, Parma and Piacenza left in 1500-1512 under French rule, Brescia in 1426.)

17,546 km2, the same outline as 1526 (a 24 km2 boundary refinement). Francesco 'was permitted to return to Milan' for 900,000 scudi after the Treaty of Cambrai (signed 3 August 1529); the page says Sforza ceded no territory.

The same 17,546 km2 outline. 'Francesco II Sforza died without heirs in 1535' and Charles V took control, so the Sforza duchy ends in 1535, not 1539; 1536-1539 the land is under Charles V (invested Philip on 11 October 1540).

region.text: Milan, Pavia and the Lombard-Piedmontese lands plus Verona, Vicenza, Bassano and Feltre

ledger.note: 1395: Gian Galeazzo Visconti becomes the first Duke of Milan. 'The duchy was officially established on 11 May 1395'; he 'obtained the title of Duke of Milan by means of a diploma signed in Prague by Wenceslaus of Bohemia', ratified in Milan on 5 September 1395. The pages give the title, not a boundary: the land is the Cliopatria 1402 core plus the Veneto cities his testament names.

region.text: the lordship of Pisa

ledger.note: 1399: Gian Galeazzo becomes lord of Pisa. Infobox of the Gian Galeazzo page: 'Lord of Pisa', 'Reign: 13 February 1399 - 3 September 1402', predecessor Gherardo Appiani. This is a title separate from Duke of Milan, so Pisa is recorded as a dependency, not as land of the duchy: republic-of-pisa keeps Pisa a state through 1399 (a rename under the Visconti) to its annexation by Florence in 1406. The page gives the city, not its territory; Cliopatria's Republic of Pisa shape (to 1401) is used. Repair 2026-10-25: was a gain of Pisa into the duchy.

region.text: Verona, Vicenza, Bassano and Feltre

ledger.counterpart: Visconti heirs' lordships (Filippo Maria, Gabriele Maria)
ledger.note: 1402: Gian Galeazzo dies and the Visconti state breaks up. The page says 'His empire fragmented as infighting among his successors wrecked Milan' (infobox: died 3 September 1402); the testament gave Verona, Vicenza, Bassano and Feltre to Filippo Maria. The pages do not date any single loss, so the Veneto holdings leave the duchy in 1402 as Cliopatria's 1402 outline shows. Pisa is not part of this loss: 'To his illegitimate son, Gabriele Maria, went Pisa and Crema', and the lordship of Pisa ends with the vassal_end below. Repair 2026-10-25: Pisa removed from the region.

region.text: the lordship of Pisa

ledger.note: 1402: Gian Galeazzo's lordship of Pisa ends with his death. Infobox: 'Lord of Pisa ... 13 February 1399 - 3 September 1402'; 'To his illegitimate son, Gabriele Maria, went Pisa and Crema'. Gabriele Maria holds Pisa as a separate Visconti lordship to 1406 (republic-of-pisa keyframe 1402-1405 and annexation 1406), not as part of the Duchy of Milan.

region.text: the Ligurian coast, Genoa and its riviere

ledger.note: 1421: Milan takes Genoa. The footnote of the Wars in Lombardy page: 'Milan controlled Genoa since 1421'. The page gives the year, not the month or the exact land; the Ligurian coast is the reading.

region.text: Brescia and Bergamo with their territories

ledger.note: 1426: Venice joins Florence against Milan and the war reaches Brescia. 'In 1425, Venice, persuaded by Carmagnola, intervened on Florence's side and the war spread to Lombardy'; 'In March 1426 Carmagnola incited riots in Brescia', a city he had captured for Milan. First campaign that takes ground: Brescia.

region.text: Brescia and its territory

ledger.note: 1426: the Peace of Venice gives Brescia to Venice. 'Peace of Venice (signed in Venice through the papal legate) gave Brescia to Venice', 30 December 1426; Carmagnola had retaken the city on 26 November 1426. The war goes on (Maclodio, 4 October 1427 on this page, 12 October on the Filippo Maria page).

region.text: Bergamo and Crema with their territories

ledger.note: 1429: Venice governs Bergamo and Crema. 'A Venetian governor was established at Bergamo and Crema' in 1429. The page also lists a Peace of Ferrara on 18 April 1428 but does not say it ceded Bergamo; the cession date is the page's silence, the governor's appointment the year recorded.

region.text: Brescia and Bergamo with their territories

ledger.note: 1433: the Peace of Ferrara ends the first Venetian war. 'May 1433: Peace of Ferrara, which institutionalized an unsteady status quo.' Brescia, Bergamo and Crema stay Venetian.

region.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

ledger.note: 1440: Uri conquers the Leventina. Ticino page: 'Uri conquered the Leventina Valley in 1440', and it 'was a subject of the canton of Uri until 1798'. The Old Swiss Confederacy page names the loser: 'In 1440, Uri conquered the Leventina Valley from the Visconti, dukes of Milan'. Cliopatria's Milan shapes still hold 3-4 cells of the valley until 1496, so the keyframes from 1440 subtract it. The swiss-confederation dossier (/ledger/10) draws the same event as a 15 km disc round 8.6 E 46.5 N, which resolves to one cell outside Milan's 1439 outline; the Faido-centred 20 km disc used here covers Airolo to Biasca. Repair 2026-10-25: event added.

region.text: the Ligurian coast, Genoa and its riviere

ledger.note: 1441: Milan recognises Genoa's independence. 'Peace of Cremona, 20 November 1441: Visconti recognized Genoa's independence and promised to stop interfering in Tuscany and Romagna.' Cliopatria drops Genoa in 1440; the page's silence on a 1435 revolt is recorded in the notes.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

region.text: the Visconti duchy as Cliopatria's 1440 shape draws it

ledger.note: 1447: Filippo Maria dies and Milan becomes a republic. 'died on 13 August 1447'; 'A republic was declared behind the Palace of the Commune' on the 14th (August, per the page's sources). The land passes to the Golden Ambrosian Republic. Region less the Leventina (lost to Uri in 1440).

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

region.text: the republic's remaining land: Milan and the duchy's core

ledger.note: 1450: Francesco Sforza becomes ruler of Milan and restores the duchy. 'On 22 March 1450, he had himself declared capitano del popolo' and Duke of Milan by right of his wife; the Wars in Lombardy page says Sforza entered Milan 'in triumph' in May 1450. Pavia was already his; Lodi and Piacenza were Venetian-occupied. Region less the Leventina (lost to Uri in 1440).

region.text: Lodi and Piacenza, occupied by Venice during the Ambrosian Republic

ledger.note: 1453: Lodi and Piacenza are Milan's again. The page says only that 'by late 1453 the Venetian cities left in Lombardy were Brescia, Bergamo and Crema' (the Treaty of Lodi follows in April 1454), so by then the two cities no longer belong to Venice; the date of their return is not on the pages.

region.text: the Ligurian coast, Genoa and its riviere

ledger.note: 1464: Milan conquers Genoa under Francesco Sforza. 'In 1464 Milan changed sides, conquered Genoa and held it as a fief of the French crown'; the page also gives 1463-1478 as the span of Sforza rule.

region.text: the Ligurian coast, Genoa and its riviere

ledger.note: 1478: Genoa leaves Sforza rule. The page's 'Genoa was held by the Milanese House of Sforza' in 1463-1478 and 1488-1499 gives the end year, not the event.

region.text: the Ligurian coast, Genoa and its riviere

ledger.note: 1488: Ludovico Sforza's Milan takes Genoa again. The page gives the span 1488-1499; Cliopatria's shape returns only in 1492.

minus.text: the Leventina valley, from Airolo to Biasca

region.text: the whole duchy

ledger.note: 1499: Louis XII of France conquers Milan. 'Louis XII invaded the Milanese state in 1499, driving out Ludovico il Moro'; Ludovico was 'defeated and taken prisoner in Novara in 1500'; Louis 'remained Duke of Milan until 1512' (infobox: French occupation 1499-1512). Genoa passes to the French at the same time ('under nearly continual French occupation' 1499-1528). Region less the Leventina (lost to Uri in 1440).

region.text: the duchy without Parma and Piacenza, the Valtellina and Ticino

ledger.note: 1512: Swiss troops put Maximilian Sforza on the ducal throne. '29 December 1512: Swiss mercenaries installed Maximilian Sforza as Duke of Milan', after the Holy League drove the French out of Milan in May 1512. The Swiss cantons 'de facto controlled the duchy' until 1515. The land is Cliopatria's 1526 outline; the pages give no list. Ticino, the Valtellina and Parma-Piacenza are not in this outline because they left the Milanese state under French rule or in 1512, and are recorded in other dossiers: Ticino page 'gained the town of Bellinzona and the Riviera in 1500' (Uri, Schwyz, Nidwalden) and 'In 1512 Locarno, the Maggia Valley, Lugano and Mendrisio were annexed'; Old Swiss Confederacy page 'Valtellina (1512-1797)' among subject territories (swiss-confederation /ledger/25 gives it to the Three Leagues); papal-states /ledger/22 gives Parma and Piacenza to the pope in 1512 (the Cambrai page has the pope surrender both to Francis in December 1515). After Marignano the Swiss kept 'the territories along the road that leads from the Gotthard Pass to the gates of Como' (Duchy of Milan page), i.e. land they already held. Repair 2026-10-25: the 1515 losses of Ticino and the Valtellina and the 1521 loss of Parma and Piacenza were deleted as losses of land the duchy did not hold.

region.text: the duchy of Maximilian Sforza under Swiss protection

ledger.note: 1513: the Swiss make Milan their protectorate. Marignano page: after Novara 'The Swiss had taken control of Milan' and returned Maximilian Sforza to the ducal throne 'to make Milan a protectorate of Switzerland'. The page gives no year for the restoration; the Battle of Novara is 6 June 1513 (Cambrai page) and swiss-confederation /ledger/26 dates the protectorate 1513. The Cambrai page has Swiss mercenaries install Maximilian on 29 December 1512 and says the Milanese saw him as 'a puppet of his Swiss mercenaries', so the control may begin with the installation. The land is Cliopatria's 1526 outline, as for the 1512 gain. Repair 2026-10-25: event added.

region.text: the duchy of Maximilian Sforza under Swiss protection

ledger.note: 1515: Marignano ends the Swiss protectorate. Marignano page: 'The battle ended all Swiss aspirations in Milan' (13-14 September 1515, per the Cambrai page); the Swiss Confederacy 'renounced all claims to the protectorate of Milan' in the Perpetual Peace of Fribourg, 29 November 1516. The French take Milan on 4 October 1515 (next event). Repair 2026-10-25: event added.

region.text: the duchy of Maximilian Sforza

ledger.note: 1515: the French take Milan after Marignano. '13-14 September 1515: Battle of Marignano', decisive victory for Francis and the Venetians; on 4 October 1515 'French troops captured Milan and dethroned Sforza'. The Treaty of Noyon (August 1516) confirmed France's claim to Milan.

region.text: the duchy of Francesco II Sforza

ledger.note: 1521: Lautrec is driven out of Milan. 'by late November 1521 [Lautrec] had been forced out of Milan' after the Battle of Vaprio d'Adda; Francesco II Sforza is 'restored to power' under Imperial and papal protection (the Duchy page: Charles V 'raised Maximilian's young brother, Francesco II Sforza, to the ducal throne').

region.text: Milan and the duchy

ledger.note: 1524: the French re-enter Milan. 'On 26 October [1524] he withdrew to Lodi' (Lannoy) 'and the French entered Milan'; Francis advanced 'at the head of an army numbering more than 40,000'. The page gives the day and implies the year.

region.text: Milan and the duchy

ledger.note: 1525: Pavia ends the French hold on Milan. 'On the night of 23 February, Imperial artillery began a bombardment'; Francis was captured and 'France never regained Lombardy'. The Duchy page dates Pavia 24 February 1525.

region.text: Milan and the duchy

ledger.note: 1526: Imperial troops take Milan from Sforza. 'The citadel of Milan fell to Imperial forces on 24 July 1526' in the War of the League of Cognac; the League page: 'Imperial troops marched into Lombardy and soon forced Sforza to abandon Milan'. Cliopatria keeps the duchy on the map; the land is Charles V's until 1529.

region.text: Milan and the duchy

ledger.note: 1529: Sforza returns to Milan after the Treaty of Cambrai. 'The final Treaty of Cambrai, signed on 3 August' (1529, from the infobox); Francesco 'was permitted to return to Milan' for 900,000 scudi. The page does not date the return or say that Sforza ceded territory.

region.text: the whole duchy

ledger.note: 1535: Francesco II Sforza dies without heirs and Charles V takes the duchy. 'Francesco II Sforza died without heirs in 1535'; Charles V, 'claiming it as an imperial fief', obtained control and installed his son Philip by a diploma signed in Brussels on 11 October 1540, recognised by Henry II of France in 1559.

wars.name: Wars in Lombardy

zones.text: Brescia and Bergamo with their territories

wars.outcome: Venice took Brescia (Peace of Venice, 30 December 1426) and governed Bergamo and Crema from 1429; the Peace of Ferrara (May 1433) froze the front; the Peace of Cremona (20 November 1441) freed Genoa; the Treaty of Lodi (April 1454) ended the wars with Sforza ruling Milan and Venice holding Brescia, Bergamo and Crema.
wars.note: The page gives no border terms for the Treaty of Lodi. Battle of Maclodio is 4 October 1427 on this page and 12 October on the Filippo Maria page; Peace of Ferrara appears twice (18 April 1428, May 1433).

wars.name: Louis XII's conquest of Milan
wars.outcome: Louis XII drove out Ludovico il Moro in 1499 and held the duchy until 1512; Ludovico was defeated and captured at Novara in 1500.
wars.note: Months are not on the page.

wars.name: War of the League of Cambrai

zones.text: Milan and the western Lombard cities

wars.outcome: The French lost Milan in 1512, Maximilian Sforza ruled under the Swiss from 29 December 1512, the French returned after Marignano (13-14 September 1515) and took Milan on 4 October 1515; the Treaty of Noyon (August 1516) and the Treaty of Brussels (6 December 1516) confirmed French rule.
wars.note: Years of the war itself beyond 1508 (the plan of the League) and 1516 are not on the page; the Milanese stages are.

wars.name: Italian War of 1521-1526
wars.outcome: Lautrec lost Milan in late November 1521, the French re-entered it on 26 October 1524 and lost it and the king at Pavia (23-24 February 1525); Francis renounced his Italian claims in the Treaty of Madrid (14 January 1526).
wars.note: The page does not date Sforza's installation.

wars.name: War of the League of Cognac
wars.outcome: The League of Cognac was signed on 22 May 1526; Imperial troops forced Sforza out of Milan; the Treaty of Cambrai (3 August 1529) removed France from the war and Sforza returned for 900,000 scudi.
wars.note: The siege of the Castello Sforzesco is not on this page (the Duchy page has the fall on 24 July 1526).

certainty.note: No page opened gives a treaty line for the duchy's borders; the Peace of Lodi (April 1454) is the first treaty but its terms are not on the page. The Swiss frontier after 1515 is the most settled.

notes: Pages opened: 12 against the up to 9 budgeted (9 in the first run, 3 more in the repair of 2026-10-25: Ticino, Battle of Marignano, Old Swiss Confederacy, ordered by the review; the Gian Galeazzo page was re-opened) (the Golden Ambrosian Republic page is shared with the ambrosian-republic dossier).
